takes.text: Your painkiller knows where it hurts.
It doesn't.
It seems to.
You swallow one, the ankle feels better, so the pill must have gone there.
The pill dissolves and passes into your blood.
Its level peaks within one to two hours. It sticks to blood proteins, so it mostly stays in the bloodstream.
Blood reaches every organ, and the drug travels with it.
Hurt tissue switches on an enzyme called COX-2. It makes prostaglandins.
They make nerves more sensitive to the chemicals injury releases.
Ibuprofen blocks both versions of that enzyme, everywhere it works.
The sore ankle is where that enzyme is busiest, so the block removes the most there.
The same block runs everywhere. Your stomach makes its own prostaglandins to help guard its lining.
Block it, and ulcers and bleeding can happen. The label calls them serious.
Your kidneys use prostaglandins to keep blood flowing. In people with kidney problems, ibuprofen can cut that flow.
Not every painkiller plays this game.
Paracetamol, or acetaminophen, has almost no anti-inflammatory effect.
It works mostly in the brain and spinal cord. Scientists still argue about exactly how.
Opioids like morphine work largely through the nervous system.
So it doesn't know where your pain is.
It doesn't need to. The sore spot is just the busiest factory, and the pill shuts down every factory it reaches.
